title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: "Here's Dolly for you, princess — you were so eager to see her," said Anna, coming out with Darya Alexandrovna onto the stone terrace, where Princess Varvara was sitting in the shade at an embroidery frame, working on a cover for Count Alexey Kirillovitch's easy chair. "She says she doesn't want anything before dinner, but please order her some lunch, and I'll go find Alexey and bring them all in."

Princess Varvara received Dolly cordially and rather patronizingly, and at once began to explain that she was living with Anna because she had always cared more for her than for her sister Katerina Pavlovna, the aunt who had raised Anna, and that now, when everyone else had abandoned Anna, she felt it her duty to help her through this most difficult transitional period.

"Her husband will give her a divorce, and then I shall go back to my solitude; but for now I can be useful, and I am doing my duty, however hard it is for me — unlike certain others. And how lovely of you, how right of you to have come! They live like the best of married couples; it's for God to judge them, not for us. And didn't Biryuzovsky and Madame Avenieva... and Sam Nikandrov, and Vassiliev and Madame Mamonova, and Liza Neptunova.... Did no one ever say a word about them? And it ended with all of them being received everywhere. And then, _c'est un intérieur si joli, si comme il faut. Tout-à-fait à l'anglaise. On se réunit le matin au breakfast, et puis on se sépare._ Everyone does whatever he likes until dinner. Dinner at seven. Stiva did very rightly to send you. He needs their support. You know that through his mother and his brother Alexey can do anything. And then they do so much good. Hasn't he told you about his hospital? _Ce sera admirable_ — everything from Paris."

Their conversation was cut short by Anna, who had found the men of the party in the billiard room and was coming back with them to the terrace. There was still a long time before dinner, the weather was exquisite, and several different ways of spending the next two hours were proposed. There were a great many ways to pass the time at Vozdvizhenskoe, and all of them were unlike those at Pokrovskoe.
"_Une partie de lawn-tennis_," Veslovsky proposed, with his handsome smile. "We'll be partners again, Anna Arkadyevna."
"No, it's too hot; better to stroll about the garden and take a row in the boat, and show Darya Alexandrovna the riverbanks," Vronsky proposed.
"I'm in for anything," said Sviazhsky.
"I imagine what Dolly would like best would be a walk — wouldn't you? And then the boat, perhaps," said Anna.
And so it was decided. Veslovsky and Tushkevitch went off to the bathing place, promising to ready the boat and to wait there for the others.

They walked along the path in two pairs — Anna with Sviazhsky, and Dolly with Vronsky. Dolly felt a little awkward and anxious in this new setting. In the abstract, in theory, she did not merely defend Anna's behavior; she positively approved of it. As is in fact not uncommon with women of impeccable virtue, weary of the monotony of respectable life, at a distance she had not only excused illicit love but actually envied it. Besides, she loved Anna with all her heart. But seeing Anna in real life among these strangers, in this fashionable tone so unfamiliar to her, she felt uneasy. What she particularly disliked was watching Princess Varvara ready to overlook anything for the sake of the comforts she enjoyed.

As a general principle, in the abstract, Dolly approved of Anna's choice; but to see the man for whose sake the choice had been made was unpleasant to her. Besides, she had never liked Vronsky. She thought him very proud, and saw nothing in him to be proud of except his wealth. But against her will, here in his own house, he intimidated her more than ever, and she could not be at ease with him. With him she felt the same thing she had felt with the maid about her dressing jacket. Just as with the maid she had felt not exactly ashamed, but embarrassed, by her darns, so with him she felt not exactly ashamed, but embarrassed, by herself.

Dolly felt awkward and cast about for something to talk about. Even though she supposed that, given his pride, praise of his house and garden would be sure to displease him, she told him anyway how very much she liked his house.
"Yes, it's a very fine building, and in the good old style," he said.
"I like the courtyard in front of the steps so much. Has it always been like that?"
"Oh, no!" he said, his face lighting up with pleasure. "If you could only have seen that courtyard last spring!"

And he began — at first rather diffidently, then more and more carried away by the subject — to point out to her the various details of the decoration of his house and garden. It was clear that, having put a great deal of effort into improving and beautifying his home, Vronsky felt a need to show off those improvements to someone new, and that he was genuinely delighted by Darya Alexandrovna's praise.
"If you'd care to see the hospital, and you aren't tired — it's really not far. Shall we go?" he said, glancing at her face to make sure she wasn't bored. "Are you coming, Anna?" he turned to her.
"We will, won't we?" she said, turning to Sviazhsky. "_Mais il ne faut pas laisser le pauvre Veslovsky et Tushkevitch se morfondre là dans le bateau._ We had better send someone to let them know."
"Yes, this is a monument he is putting up for himself here," Anna said, turning to Dolly with that same sly, knowing smile she had worn earlier when talking about the hospital.
"Oh, it's a real and important piece of work!" said Sviazhsky. But to show he wasn't trying to flatter Vronsky, he promptly added a few mildly critical remarks.
"Still, I do wonder, count," he said, "that while you do so much for the peasants' health, you take so little interest in the schools."

"_C'est devenu tellement commun les écoles_," said Vronsky. "You understand, it's not on principle — it just happens that my interest has been drawn elsewhere. This way to the hospital, then," he said to Darya Alexandrovna, pointing to a turning off the avenue.

The ladies put up their parasols and turned onto the side path. After several turnings, and through a small gate, Darya Alexandrovna saw, on a rise ahead of her, a large, rather pretentious red building, almost finished. The iron roof, still unpainted, glittered blindingly in the sunshine. Next to the completed building another had been begun, ringed with scaffolding. Workmen in aprons stood on the scaffolds, laying bricks, pouring mortar out of vats, and smoothing it with trowels.
"How quickly the work gets done here!" said Sviazhsky. "Last time I was here, the roof wasn't on yet."
"By autumn it will all be ready. Inside, almost everything is done," said Anna.
"And what's this new building?"

"That's where the doctor will live, and the dispensary," Vronsky said, spotting the architect in a short jacket walking up to him; and with a word of apology to the ladies, he stepped away to meet him.
Going around a pit where the workmen were slaking lime, he stopped with the architect and began to talk rather warmly.
"The front is still too low," he said to Anna, who had asked what the matter was.
"I said the foundation ought to have been raised," said Anna.
"Yes, of course it would have been much better, Anna Arkadyevna," the architect said, "but now it is too late."

"Yes, I take a great interest in it," Anna said in answer to Sviazhsky, who was expressing his surprise at her grasp of architecture. "This new building should have been in keeping with the hospital. It was an afterthought, and was begun without a plan."
Having finished his talk with the architect, Vronsky rejoined the ladies and led them into the hospital.

Although the cornices outside were still being worked on and the ground floor was being painted, upstairs almost all of the rooms were finished. Going up the broad cast-iron staircase to the landing, they walked into the first large room. The walls were stuccoed to look like marble; the huge plate-glass windows were already in; only the parquet floor was still unfinished, and the carpenters, who had been planing a block of it, left their work, took off the bands that tied back their hair, and bowed to the gentry.
"This is the reception room," Vronsky said. "There will be a desk in here, some tables, and benches, and nothing more."
"This way; let's go in here. Don't go near the window," said Anna, touching the paint to see whether it was dry. "Alexey, the paint's dry already," she added.

From the reception room they went into the corridor. Here Vronsky showed them the ventilation system, which was of a new pattern. Then he showed them the marble baths and beds with extraordinary springs. Then he took them through the wards one by one, the storeroom, the linen room, and then the heating stove of a new design, and the trolleys that would carry everything needed silently along the corridors, and many other things besides. Sviazhsky, a connoisseur of the latest mechanical improvements, took it all in with appreciation. Dolly simply marveled at all she had never seen before, and, anxious to understand it all, asked detailed questions about everything, to Vronsky's great satisfaction.
"Yes, I imagine this will be the only properly equipped hospital in Russia," said Sviazhsky.
"And aren't you going to have a maternity ward?" Dolly asked. "That's so badly needed in the country. I have so often...."
Despite his usual courtesy, Vronsky cut her off.

"This is not a maternity home, but a hospital for the sick, and it's meant for all conditions, except contagious ones," he said. "Ah! look at this," and he rolled an invalid chair, just ordered for convalescents, over to Darya Alexandrovna. "Look." He sat down in it and started moving it. "The patient can't walk — still too weak, perhaps, or with something wrong with his legs — but he needs air, and so he can move himself, roll himself along...."

Darya Alexandrovna was interested by it all. She liked everything very much, but most of all she liked Vronsky himself, with his natural, simple-hearted enthusiasm. "Yes, he's a very nice, good man," she thought several times, not hearing what he said but watching him and taking in his expression, while she mentally put herself in Anna's place. She liked him so much, just then, with his eager interest, that she saw how Anna could be in love with him.
